{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=intrinsic+motivation+metrics+benchmark+goal+generation+autonomous+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"title\": [\"Beyond Human-Designed Objectives: Autonomous Goal Generation in AI Through Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Directed Agency\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Current artificial intelligence systems remain fundamentally constrained by their dependence on human-designed objectives and reward functions, limiting their capacity for genuine autonomy and open-ended development. This paper proposes Autonomous Goal Generation Networks (AGGNs), a theoretical framework for architectures that synthesize, evaluate, and pursue their own objectives through intrinsic motivation. The framework specifies five components: Goal-Generative Networks (GGNs, based on a VAE-style sampler over a goal embedding space), Objective Evaluation Systems (OESs) with six explicit criteria, Intrinsic Motivation Engines (IMEs) implementing curiosity, competence, empowerment, autonomy, and aesthetic drives, Autonomous Agency Controllers (AACs) for concurrent-objective scheduling, and Self-Reflective Goal Refinement (SRGR) for closing the loop. We prove a goal-distribution convergence result (Theorem 1) under stationary feedback and a stability condition for the SRGR loop. The contribution of this paper is theoretical: we identify the structural and motivational ingredients an autonomously-goal-generating agent must possess. No empirical validation is reported. Section VI specifies the protocol — benchmarks (Minecraft-like exploration, creative reasoning, robotic skill acquisition, scientific discovery, multi-agent social tasks), baselines (curiosity-driven exploration, empowerment maximization, novelty search), and metrics (goal diversity, coherence, achievement rate, exploration efficiency) — against which AGGNs should be evaluated.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0905.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1609/aaai.v32i1.12195\", \"title\": [\"Adversarial Goal Generation for Intrinsic Motivation\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>\\n      \\n        Generally in Reinforcement Learning the goal, or reward sign…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=automated+reasoning+self+correction+false+premises+validation+failure+modes&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9780203435854-18\", \"title\": [\"Conditional reasoning with false premises\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203435854-18\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2002, 9, 26]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"title\": [\"Automated Oversight Diagnostic Self-Correction and Failure-Aware Reasoning for GUI Agents(ChinaMM)\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid evolution of Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) has significantly advanced autonomous GUI agents. However, during the development of GUI agents for dynamic scenarios, error compounding leads to a labor-intensive and expensive bottleneck, requiring high costs for manual intervention. Meanwhile, errors are hard to be located and difficult to track failure reasoning. Consequently, it is challenging to overcome random errors simply by blindly increasing the size of the training dataset and address errors in a targeted manner. Existing research primarily attempt to improve GUI agent by optimizing the agent&apos;s internal design to avoid outcome deviation, ignoring the critical need for automated self-correction in step-level agent errors. In view of this, we propose the Automated Oversight (AO), an efficient four-stage closed-loop approach designed to emulate human-level oversight. The architecture consists of four key phases: (1) global outcome verification for final-state checking; (2) step-level visual trajectory alignment to intercept errors in real-time; (3) teacher-driven root-cause diagnosis to analyze failures; and (4) closed-loop rectification with state rollback to recover the task. Unlike traditional methods, AO focuses on failure-aware reasoning to identify the root causes of errors and execute targeted recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can improve agent success rates and reduce human cognitive burden by achieving reliable autonomous interactions in dynamic systems. We will publicly release our code.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9780203435854_chapter_13\", \"…

Towards the formal verification of autonomous agent teams\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1049/ic:20050184\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2005]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1049/ic:20050177\", \"title\": [\"Principles, architectures and trends in autonomous control\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1049/ic:20050177\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2005]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/tmlz4501\", \"title\": [\"State-Space Reduction Techniques in Agent Verification\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>We have developed a set of tools to allow the use of model-checking techniques for the verification of systems directly implemented in an agent-oriented programming language. The success of model checking as a verification technique for large systems is dependent partly on its use in combination with various state-space reduction techniques. An important example of such techniques is property-based slicing. This paper introduces an algorithm for property-based slicing of AgentSpeak multi-agent systems. We apply our approach to the AgentSpeak code for a scenario inspired by routine tasks of autonomous Mars rovers, and explain how slicing reduces the search space in theory. We consider experiments on such scenarios, and initial results show a significant reduction in the state space, thus indicating that this approach can have an important impact on the practicality of agent verification.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/tmlz4501\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2004, 7, 19]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "22fd0be4436dd6364c5b402c5365363dd58ed420575f52cc9f14a96b4ffe0dd3", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.70729/ijser15932", "doi:10.1049/ic:20050184", "doi:10…

Automating scientific discovery requires more than generating papers from ideas. Real research is
iterative: hypotheses are challenged from multiple perspectives, experiments fail and inform the next
attempt, and lessons accumulate across cycles. Existing autonomous research systems often model
this process as a linear pipeline: they rely on single-agent reasoning, stop when execution fails, and
do not carry experience across runs. We presentAutoResearchClaw, a multi-agent autonomous
research pipeline built on five mechanisms: structured multi-agent debate for hypothesis generation and
result analysis, a self-healing executor with aPivot/Refinedecision loop that transforms failures into
information, verifiable result reporting that prevents fabricated numbers and hallucinated citations,
human-in-the-loop collaboration with seven intervention modes spanning full autonomy to step-by-step
oversight, and cross-run evolution that converts past mistakes into future safeguards. OnARC-Bench,
a 25-topic experiment-stage benchmark,AutoResearchClawoutperforms AI Scientist v2 by 54.7%. A
human-in-the-loop ablation across seven intervention modes reveals that precise, targeted collaboration
at high-leverage decision points consistently outperforms both full autonomy and exhaustive step-by-step
